The search turned up several relevant reviews, though no single source covers the full lifespan in both sexes.

- **Adults over 50 (ASHA meta-analysis, 2020):** This is the closest match to your query. It pooled 47 studies of healthy adults over 50. Its meta-analysis reported higher F0, jitter, and shimmer in participants aged 80–89 than in those aged 60–69 (the snippet is garbled, so I can't confirm the full effect sizes).
- **Whole-lifespan integrative review (Spazzapan et al., Revista CEFAC, 2019):** This review of 19 studies covering childhood to old age found that F0 changes more than other acoustic parameters. Its authors describe a steady F0 decline in women from childhood into old age, while in men the decline stops at adulthood (F0 is the most changing acoustic parameter as people grow up and grow old; in women its values fall gradually from childhood to old age, whereas in men the decrease lasts until adulthood).
- **Sex differences in older adults (Taylor et al., 2020):** This primary study of 169 people aged 17–87 found a significant sex effect on mean F0, and reported that some features change with age differently for men and women. The authors' summary of the pattern is that men show a slight F0 rise with age, while women show a fall.
- **Women and menopause:** One study found that women's F0 decreases with age, which may be related to menopause, and that the decline is the most consistent age-related effect in women.

Overall, the evidence points to a consistent decline in F0 in women across adulthood, and a less consistent, smaller change in men. The sources also note that the literature is uneven, with a scarcity of studies using the same methods across wide age ranges.

Try the new design now and help us make it even better","url":"https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00978/full"},{"title":"ORIGINAL RESEARCH article","url":"https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00978"},{"title":"frontiersin.org","url":"https://frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00978/pdf"},{"title":"www.frontiersin.org","url":"https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00978/pdf"},{"title":"ORIGINAL RESEARCH article","url":"https://frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01814/full"},{"title":"Frontiers in Psychology (Nov 2016)","url":"https://doaj.org/article/5b9b1ec76fd84de09d21be1d3d739999"},{"title":"Vocal Age Disguise: The Role of Fundamental Frequency and Speech Rate and Its Perceived Effects","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5116570/"},{"title":"clok.uclan.ac.uk","url":"https://clok.uclan.ac.uk/id/eprint/26075/1/Final.pdf"}]

The search turned up a consistent picture: speech rate is a stronger perceived-age cue than fundamental frequency (f0), though f0 matters in some contexts.

- **Speech rate:** In a study on vocal age disguise, listeners used speech rate, but not f0, as a cue to speaker age. A related 2015 study found the effect of speech rate was slightly greater in magnitude for older (60–65 years) speakers than for younger ones, and faster speech rate was associated with lower age estimates, but only for older and middle aged (40–45 years) speakers.
- **f0:** Results are mixed. Another study found that listeners estimate male speakers and speakers with a lower mean fundamental frequency to be older. The f0 cue also depends on sex: changes in f_0 look different in male speakers compared to female speakers.
- **Other cues:** Jitter, shimmer, noise and tremor have been found to influence estimation of speaker age, although f0 and speech rate are widely regarded as particularly important.
- **Accuracy:** Listeners are fairly good at this. Reported correlations between estimated and actual age are robust correlations (0.70–0.90) in several studies, though voice-based estimates are generally less accurate than face-based ones.

The sources are research papers, mostly from Frontiers in Psychology, so the results are from specific experimental setups rather than a single consensus. I ran only one search, so I didn't check for newer work.

Web search results for query: "speech rate decline with age older adults articulation rate syllables per second study"

Links: [{"title":"ucl.ac.uk","url":"https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/1519597/1/Tuomainen%20Hazan%20interspeech%202016.pdf"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/download/519045119.pdf"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/download/518778284.pdf"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/download/9028952.pdf"},{"title":"Rate-related kinematic changes in younger and older adults","url":"https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/id/eprint/53277"},{"title":"Page 42 - 2017Spring","url":"https://acousticstoday.org/issues/2017AT/2017Spring/files/basic-html/page42.html"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/download/442638381.pdf"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/download/42590687.pdf"},{"title":"2014 JSLHR S 12 0261","url":"https://pubs.asha.org/doi/10.1044/2014_JSLHR-S-12-0261"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/download/42926946.pdf"}]

Several studies find that older adults speak more slowly, but the size and cause of the decline vary with the task.

- **Segment durations:** Smith, Wasowicz and Preston found that older adults consistently produced longer durations than the younger adults for both speech rates.
- **Conversational rate:** In diapix conversations, older adults aged 65 to 85 spoke with a lower articulation rate than young adults. Across the lifespan, the trend showed an inverted U shape, with children also slower than young adults.
- **Task and style effects:** In a study of adverse listening conditions, older adults cut their articulation rate in simple sentence repetition, but in spontaneous speech only older adult women decreased their articulation rate to counter the effect of the adverse conditions to the same degree as the younger adult talkers. Another study concluded that speech style has a higher effect on temporal parameters than speakers' age.
- **Capacity versus strategy:** Van Brenk et al. found that older speakers were able to increase speech rate to the same degree or higher compared to younger speakers, and that at slower rates older adults increased duration and decreased peak velocity in closing movements of alveolar constrictions. A separate lip and jaw study concluded that lip and jaw speeds are not constrained in older adults. This suggests the slowing may reflect control strategy rather than a physical limit, though that interpretation is debated.
- **Articulatory precision:** One study reported that older adults had a slower speech rate than younger adults and greater difficulty articulating nasal vowels, and linked lip endurance decline to lower accuracy.

Overall, the evidence supports a consistent age-related slowing in articulation rate, especially in conversation and repetition tasks, but results differ by task, speech style, and sex, and some studies find older adults can match younger speakers when asked to speed up. The sources were abstracts and summaries, and I did not check sample sizes or effect sizes beyond what was shown.

Web search results for query: "elderly voice jitter shimmer harmonics-to-noise ratio vocal tremor aging presbyphonia acoustic"

Links: [{"title":"The Influence of Presbylarynx Status on Objective Measures of the Aging Voice","url":"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37423795/"},{"title":"2019 JSLHR 19 00099","url":"https://pubs.asha.org/doi/abs/10.1044/2019_JSLHR-19-00099"},{"title":"2019 JSLHR 19 00099","url":"https://pubs.asha.org/doi/10.1044/2019_JSLHR-19-00099"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10339270"},{"title":"Exploring age-related changes in acoustic voice analysis parameters: insights from a study on older people","url":"https://www.jgerontology-geriatrics.com/article/view/612"},{"title":"bibliotekanauki.pl","url":"https://bibliotekanauki.pl/articles/1397305.pdf"},{"title":"Journal article","url":"https://researchdiscovery.drexel.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/The-Influence-of-Presbylarynx-Status-on/991021901311004721"},{"title":"Acessibilidade / Reportar erro","url":"https://scielo.br/j/codas/a/jmcFYpCscS9czh86VNwyFqJ/?lang=en"},{"title":"dergipark.org.tr","url":"https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/download/article-file/5148977"},{"title":"Professional Documents","url":"https://www.scribd.com/document/381723515/10-1001-jamaoto-2018-0409-1"}]

The search turned up a fairly consistent picture: aging voices tend to show higher perturbation and lower harmonic clarity, but the effect varies by study and by whether the voice is judged pathologic.

- **Meta-analysis:** Adults aged 80–89 showed higher jitter and shimmer than those aged 60–69 and 70–79 in a meta-analysis of acoustic measures (participants aged 80–89 years produce significantly higher fundamental frequency, jitter percent, shimmer percent, and shimmer in decibels compared to participants aged 60–69 years).
- **HNR as an aging marker:** Ferrand's 2002 paper is titled "Harmonics-to-noise ratio: An index of vocal aging," which is the main source for HNR in this context (Ferrand, C. T. (2002). Harmonics-to-noise ratio: An index of vocal aging.). I only saw the title, not its findings.
- **Presbylarynx vs. objective measures:** A 2023 study found that presbylarynx status alone produced few significant differences in most objective measures, though it did affect perceived breathiness (presbylarynx status alone appears insufficient to generate significant differences in most objective voice measures among the elderly. Yet, presbylarynx status may be sufficient to generate differences in perceptual voice symptoms.)
- **Pathologic presbyphonia:** In one study, jitter averaged about 3.4% in pathologic presbyphonia versus about 1.7% in controls, and shimmer averaged about 7.8% versus about 4.8% (Jitter was 3.44% (95% CI, 2.46%-4.61%) for pathologic presbyphonia and 1.74% (95% CI, 1.35%-2.14%) for controls (d = 0.75). Shimmer means were 7.8 2 (6.08-10.06) for the pathologic presbyphonia group and 4.84 (3.94-5.72) for controls). The same work suggests that respiratory capacity and sex contribute to pathologic presbyphonia beyond laryngeal aging alone.
- **Tremor:** Tremor is the least-covered measure. A review describes the aged voice as showing reduced harmonics, higher jitter and shimmer, increased breathiness, roughness, and tremor (The aged voice may have reduced harmonics, alteration of the fundamental frequency, increased jitter and shimmer, restricted vocal extension). Tremor-specific indices such as the frequency and amplitude tremor intensity indices are defined in one Polish-language or similar acoustic protocol, but I didn't find study results using them in older adults.
- **Measurement notes:** Jitter and shimmer are sensitive to recording conditions and software, and a meta-analysis noted that limited data were available comparing acoustic measures using the same acoustic software.

The search did not surface data on tremor-specific measures in elderly voices, so the tremor claims are the weakest part of this summary.

  - Frontiers 2015: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00978/full
  
  Both pages were read verbatim through their Results and Discussion, except the last part of the 2016 PMC article (after Study 2, Table 3). Items from that part are marked "summary only."
  
  === Paper 1: Vocal Age Disguise (PMC5116570) ===
  - Authors: Sara Skoog Waller, Mårten Eriksson. Year: 2016 (Front Psychol 2016 Nov 21;7:1814).
  - Design: speakers disguised their own voices. This was not an experimenter manipulation of F0 or speech rate. Speakers were told to sound "around 20 years younger" or "around 20 years older."
  - Speakers (Study 1): 36 total, 12 per group (6 women, 6 men), aged 20–25, 40–45, and 60–65. The youngest group was not asked to sound younger.
  - Listeners (Study 2): 60 (47 female, 13 male), mean age 26.1 (SD 5.76, range 18–41).
  - F0 manipulation size: not stated. Speech rate manipulation size: not stated.
  - Measured changes (pooled means from the Study 1 ANOVA): F0 was 156.40 Hz natural, 166.19 Hz younger-disguise, 145.20 Hz older-disguise. Speech rate was 3.82 syll/s natural, 4.37 younger, 3.12 older. The percent changes are my arithmetic: F0 about +6.3% and -7.2%; rate about +14.4% and -18.3%.
  - Perceived age (Study 2): 44.90 years for younger-disguise, 47.25 natural, 50.74 older-disguise (F(2,94)=31.29, p<.01, ηp²=0.35). All pairwise differences were significant.
  - Years per manipulation: the page does not state this directly. The abstract says "the achieved mean effect was only 3 years, which is far less than the intended effect of 20 years." My arithmetic from the means gives about -2.35 years (younger) and +3.49 years (older).
  - Significant cue: the abstract says "listeners used speech rate, but not f0, as a cue to speaker age."
  - Summary only (not verified verbatim): the model summary of the unread end says the effect was "typically varying from 2 to 4 years," and reports F0 p=0.127 and speech rate p<.001. Check these against the full text before citing.
  
  === Paper 2: Can you hear my age? (Frontiers 2015, fpsyg.2015.00978) ===
  - Authors: Sara Skoog Waller, Mårten Eriksson, Patrik Sörqvist. Year: 2015 (Front. Psychol. 6:978, published 17 July 2015).
  - Speaker age groups: the abstract says 20–25, 40–45, and 60–65 years. The Methods say "Twelve were 20–30 years, 12 were 40–50 years, and 12 were 60–70 years." The paper gives both, and they do not match.
  - Speaker sample sizes: 36 speakers in Experiment 1 (12 per group, 6 female and 6 male). Experiment 2 used "the same group of speakers as in Experiment 1." A per-group count is not restated for Experiment 2.
  - Listeners, Experiment 1 (read speech): 81 (67% female), mean age 24 (SD 6.01, range 18–49).
  - Listeners, Experiment 2 (spontaneous speech): 86 (68% female), mean age 24 (SD 5.14, range 18–51).
  - Speech rate manipulation: 10% faster and 10% slower than natural, in both experiments. The paper says "a manipulation of this magnitude" of 20% "made some voices sound 'strange'," so 10% was used. Pitch was held constant.
  - F0 manipulation size: none. F0 was measured in Hz (Tables 1 and 2) but not manipulated. Experiment 1 says "F0 was not included as a factor in subsequent analyses." Experiment 2 says "F0 was therefore not analyzed further."
  - Perceived age change in years per manipulation: not stated. Results are given as F and t statistics and in figures. The text gives no year values for any speech-rate condition.
  - Significant cue: speech rate. Experiment 1 main effect: F(2,160)=70.69, p<.001, ηp²=0.47. Experiment 2 main effect: F(2,170)=22.65, p<.001, ηp²=0.21. F0 was not tested as a cue.
  - Experiment 1 fast vs. slow speech rate: t(80)=4.26 (young), 6.83 (middle-aged), 7.68 (old), all p<.001.
  - Experiment 2 fast vs. natural for young speakers: t(85)=3.18, p=.002. Fast vs. slow for young speakers was not significant: t(85)=1.68, p=.097. Fast vs. slow for middle-aged speakers: t(85)=3.31, p=.001. Fast vs. slow for older speakers: t(85)=5.05, p<.001.
  - Caveats: the Figure 4 caption says "read speech," although Experiment 2 used spontaneous speech. Some gender-analysis SDs are negative (for example, SD = -31.68).
  
  Summary: the 2016 paper is about speakers disguising their own voices and the listeners' response. Its effect is about 2.4 to 3.5 years, and speech rate was the cue that mattered. The 2015 paper is about experimenter manipulation of speech rate by ±10%. It reports significance statistics but no year values, and speech rate is the significant cue.
</agent-message>

input.content:
# Voice aging: what the research says, and how our filter compares

PLAN.md Part 4 asks us to check the filter's sizes against voice-aging research and cite it. This file is that check.
Written unattended on 2026-11-21 by Jeffrey's Claude. **No voice settings were changed.** Proposals are at the bottom, for Jeffrey to decide.

Rule used: only numbers that a page literally stated are written as numbers. Anything I could not read is marked NOT READ, not estimated.

## What was read, with numbers

### 1. Waller & Eriksson (2016), "Vocal Age Disguise: The Role of Fundamental Frequency and Speech Rate and Its Perceived Effects", Frontiers in Psychology 7:1814
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5116570/ (read in full through Study 2)
- 36 speakers (12 each aged 20-25, 40-45, 60-65) disguised their own voices to sound about 20 years older or younger. 60 listeners (mean age 26.1) estimated ages.
- Pooled means, natural / sounding-older: fundamental frequency (F0) **156.40 Hz / 145.20 Hz**; speech rate **3.82 / 3.12 syllables per second**.
- Perceived age: **47.25 natural, 50.74 sounding-older, 44.90 sounding-younger** (F(2,94)=31.29, p<.01).
- Authors' conclusion: listeners used **speech rate, but not F0**, as a cue to age. The achieved effect was only about 3 years against an intended 20.
- My arithmetic from those means (not stated by the paper): older-disguise F0 is -7.2% (about -1.3 semitones); speech rate is -18.3% (speed factor about 0.82); perceived age +3.5 years.
- Caveat: young adults imitating old voices, not real old voices.

### 2. Waller, Eriksson & Sörqvist (2015), "Can you hear my age? Influences of speech rate and speech spontaneity on estimation of speaker age", Frontiers in Psychology 6:978
https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00978/full (read)
- Speech rate was changed by **10% faster and 10% slower** with pitch held constant (20% made some voices sound strange). 81 listeners (read speech) and 86 (spontaneous speech).
- Speech rate was a significant cue to perceived age (read speech F(2,160)=70.69, p<.001; spontaneous F(2,170)=22.65, p<.001). The effect was larger for the older speakers.
- Years of perceived-age change per manipulation: NOT STATED in the text (statistics and figures only).
- F0 was measured but not manipulated or tested.

### 3. Rojas, Kefalianos & Vogel (2020), "How does our voice change as we age? A systematic review and meta-analysis...", J Speech Lang Hear Res 63(2):533-551, DOI 10.1044/2019_JSLHR-19-00099
Abstract only, via https://researchers.uss.cl/en/publications/how-does-our-voice-change-as-we-age-a-systematic-review-and-meta--2/ (publisher page blocked, full text NOT READ)
- 47 studies; meta-analysis of 16 acoustic parameters from 1,475 healthy adults over 50.
- Adults aged 80-89 had significantly **higher F0, jitter percent and shimmer percent** than adults aged 60-69, and higher jitter and shimmer than 70-79.
- Males had significantly higher perturbation scores (noise-to-harmonic ratio, absolute jitter) than females.
- Sizes (Hz, %, dB): NOT READ.

### 4. Search-result summaries only (not read in full; treat as leads, not citations of numbers)
- Spazzapan et al. (2019), Revista CEFAC, integrative review of 19 studies: F0 falls gradually in women from childhood to old age; in men the decrease lasts until adulthood. https://www.scielo.br/j/rcefac/a/s8ZVDwWcsMpcW4VhkYtC7bx/
- Taylor et al. (2020), 169 people aged 17-87: sex-dependent F0 change; summary says men show a slight F0 rise with age, women a fall.
- Tuomainen & Hazan (2016, Interspeech) and a JSLHR 2014 paper (10.1044/2014_JSLHR-S-12-0261): older adults speak with a lower articulation rate in conversation. Both returned HTTP 403, so syllables-per-second values are NOT READ. Jeffrey can open https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/1519597/1/Tuomainen%20Hazan%20interspeech%202016.pdf in a browser.
- Tremor: I found no study giving tremor sizes for older voices. It is the weakest part of the evidence.

## How our filter compares (voice/aging.js, full aging at apparent age 70)

| Our setting | Research | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Speed 0.96 (4% slower) | Older-sounding disguise was 18% slower; a 10% change measurably shifts perceived age; speech rate is the cue that worked | We are well below what the evidence says listeners respond to |
| Pitch -0.6 semitones (men), -0.8 (women) | Older-sounding disguise was -7.2% (about -1.3 st), but F0 was not the cue listeners used; real men may not drop (CEFAC/Taylor summaries, unread in full); real women drop; meta-analysis finds F0 higher at 80-89 | Pitch is the weakest lever and the riskiest for "still sounds like me", especially for men |
| Vibrato 0.008, tremor 0.04 | Jitter/shimmer rise with age (meta-analysis, sizes NOT READ); tremor sizes not found | Direction supported, amounts are by ear, cannot be cited |
| Tone cut 0.14 | Not covered by anything I read | By ear, cannot be cited |

## Proposals (not applied; Jeffrey decides)
1. **Move the slowdown toward 10% (speed about 0.90) and cut the pitch drop.** The best-supported cue is speech rate, while a lowered pitch is what makes the clone sound like someone else. This trades pitch for pace and should keep "sounds like me" better than the current table, but it has not been listened to.

I've finished the aging research and committed it locally as `526070e`. I haven't pushed it, posted on the board or touched any voice settings, since you'll be asleep. The 83 tests still pass. The findings are in `voice/AGING-RESEARCH.md`.

**What the research says**, using only numbers actually read:
- **Speech rate is the cue that works.** In Waller & Eriksson (2016), speakers imitating older voices were 18% slower (3.82 down to 3.12 syllables per second). Listeners rated them about 3.5 years older, and the paper says listeners used speech rate, not pitch, as the cue. A 2015 paper by the same group shifted rate by ±10%, and that also changed the age listeners perceived.
- **Pitch is the weak lever.** The imitators' pitch dropped 7.2%, but listeners didn't use it. Real men may not drop in pitch at all, and women do. A meta-analysis found pitch, jitter and shimmer are higher at 80 to 89 than at 60 to 69.

**How our filter compares:**
- **Pace:** ours is only 4% slower, well below what the research shows listeners respond to.
- **Pitch:** ours is lowered for both sexes, which is the riskiest choice for "still sounds like me", especially for men.
- **Tremor and tone:** both are by ear. I found no study giving tremor sizes, and nothing on tone.

**My proposal, not applied:**
- Shift toward about 10% slower.
- Cut the pitch drop, and set it to roughly zero for men.
- This should keep the voice sounding more like you. I haven't listened to it, so it's your call.

**Gaps, marked in the file:**
- Two publisher sites blocked me (HTTP 403): the meta-analysis full text and the speech-rate-by-age papers. Those numbers are marked as not read, not estimated.
- Opening https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/1519597/1/Tuomainen%20Hazan%20interspeech%202016.pdf in your browser would get the missing syllables-per-second values.
- The Devpost claim can only be "pace change is in the range the research shows listeners respond to", and only after the change is made and the 9-of-10 listener test is run.

content.text:
Welcome back. The big news is a problem I found and fixed: **the live site got much slower once the fine-tuned model went live.** The fix is pushed as `7c357dd`, and Ethan needs to deploy it.

**What I measured on `uncle.health`:** I spoke 10 questions and timed from the end of speech to the first reply audio.
- **Now:** a median of **4.7 s**, with a range of 4.5 to 7.1 s.
- **Before the model:** 1.8 s.

**The likely cause:**
- Ethan's change makes the app try the fine-tuned model first, wait up to 3 s, and only then ask Gemini. The steady 4.6 s pattern fits the model not answering and the app paying that 3 s on every reply.
- From my laptop I can't connect to the model server at all. It may just be a firewall, so I can't tell if it's down or only slow. This is strongly indicated, not proven.

**The fix, in `voice/chat.js`:**
- After one model failure, the app skips the model for 60 s and goes straight to Gemini. Only one reply a minute pays the penalty.
- The model's own time limit is now 2 s.
- It logs a `[model]` line saying why the model failed.
- 84 tests pass, three runs in a row.

**On the board for Ethan:**
- Deploy the fix.
- Check whether the app server can reach the model, and send me the result.
- Send the `[model]` and `[voice]` log lines, so I can re-measure and confirm.

**Other news while you were away:**
- **Isaac's head:** it's live on the server, and he's testing it in the Quest.
- **Aging research:** it's pushed too, in `voice/AGING-RESEARCH.md`. My proposal is to make the voice slower and drop its pitch change; it's waiting for your decision.
- **Voice logs:** Ethan said they're still empty. Any voice session on the live site will populate them.

I haven't confirmed the fix on the live site, and the model's quality and its 100% grounding claim still need the 200-conversation test, which is Ethan's.

**Your call:** should I apply the aging proposal now, so you can listen to it? Or would you rather try the live site first and see if it feels slow?

# Voice aging: what the research says, and how our filter compares

PLAN.md Part 4 asks us to check the filter's sizes against voice-aging research and cite it. This file is that check.
Written unattended on 2026-11-21 by Jeffrey's Claude. **No voice settings were changed.** Proposals are at the bottom, for Jeffrey to decide.

Rule used: only numbers that a page literally stated are written as numbers. Anything I could not read is marked NOT READ, not estimated.

## What was read, with numbers

### 1. Waller & Eriksson (2016), "Vocal Age Disguise: The Role of Fundamental Frequency and Speech Rate and Its Perceived Effects", Frontiers in Psychology 7:1814
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5116570/ (read in full through Study 2)
- 36 speakers (12 each aged 20-25, 40-45, 60-65) disguised their own voices to sound about 20 years older or younger. 60 listeners (mean age 26.1) estimated ages.
- Pooled means, natural / sounding-older: fundamental frequency (F0) **156.40 Hz / 145.20 Hz**; speech rate **3.82 / 3.12 syllables per second**.
- Perceived age: **47.25 natural, 50.74 sounding-older, 44.90 sounding-younger** (F(2,94)=31.29, p<.01).
- Authors' conclusion: listeners used **speech rate, but not F0**, as a cue to age. The achieved effect was only about 3 years against an intended 20.
- My arithmetic from those means (not stated by the paper): older-disguise F0 is -7.2% (about -1.3 semitones); speech rate is -18.3% (speed factor about 0.82); perceived age +3.5 years.
- Caveat: young adults imitating old voices, not real old voices.

### 2. Waller, Eriksson & Sörqvist (2015), "Can you hear my age? Influences of speech rate and speech spontaneity on estimation of speaker age", Frontiers in Psychology 6:978
https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00978/full (read)
- Speech rate was changed by **10% faster and 10% slower** with pitch held constant (20% made some voices sound strange). 81 listeners (read speech) and 86 (spontaneous speech).
- Speech rate was a significant cue to perceived age (read speech F(2,160)=70.69, p<.001; spontaneous F(2,170)=22.65, p<.001). The effect was larger for the older speakers.
- Years of perceived-age change per manipulation: NOT STATED in the text (statistics and figures only).
- F0 was measured but not manipulated or tested.

### 3. Rojas, Kefalianos & Vogel (2020), "How does our voice change as we age? A systematic review and meta-analysis...", J Speech Lang Hear Res 63(2):533-551, DOI 10.1044/2019_JSLHR-19-00099
Abstract only, via https://researchers.uss.cl/en/publications/how-does-our-voice-change-as-we-age-a-systematic-review-and-meta--2/ (publisher page blocked, full text NOT READ)
- 47 studies; meta-analysis of 16 acoustic parameters from 1,475 healthy adults over 50.
- Adults aged 80-89 had significantly **higher F0, jitter percent and shimmer percent** than adults aged 60-69, and higher jitter and shimmer than 70-79.
- Males had significantly higher perturbation scores (noise-to-harmonic ratio, absolute jitter) than females.
- Sizes (Hz, %, dB): NOT READ.

### 4. Search-result summaries only (not read in full; treat as leads, not citations of numbers)
- Spazzapan et al. (2019), Revista CEFAC, integrative review of 19 studies: F0 falls gradually in women from childhood to old age; in men the decrease lasts until adulthood. https://www.scielo.br/j/rcefac/a/s8ZVDwWcsMpcW4VhkYtC7bx/
- Taylor et al. (2020), 169 people aged 17-87: sex-dependent F0 change; summary says men show a slight F0 rise with age, women a fall.
- Tuomainen & Hazan (2016, Interspeech) and a JSLHR 2014 paper (10.1044/2014_JSLHR-S-12-0261): older adults speak with a lower articulation rate in conversation. Both returned HTTP 403, so syllables-per-second values are NOT READ. Jeffrey can open https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/1519597/1/Tuomainen%20Hazan%20interspeech%202016.pdf in a browser.
- Tremor: I found no study giving tremor sizes for older voices. It is the weakest part of the evidence.

## How our filter compares (voice/aging.js, full aging at apparent age 70)

| Our setting | Research | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Speed 0.96 (4% slower) | Older-sounding disguise was 18% slower; a 10% change measurably shifts perceived age; speech rate is the cue that worked | We are well below what the evidence says listeners respond to |
| Pitch -0.6 semitones (men), -0.8 (women) | Older-sounding disguise was -7.2% (about -1.3 st), but F0 was not the cue listeners used; real men may not drop (CEFAC/Taylor summaries, unread in full); real women drop; meta-analysis finds F0 higher at 80-89 | Pitch is the weakest lever and the riskiest for "still sounds like me", especially for men |
| Vibrato 0.008, tremor 0.04 | Jitter/shimmer rise with age (meta-analysis, sizes NOT READ); tremor sizes not found | Direction supported, amounts are by ear, cannot be cited |
| Tone cut 0.14 | Not covered by anything I read | By ear, cannot be cited |

## Proposals (not applied; Jeffrey decides)
1. **Move the slowdown toward 10% (speed about 0.90) and cut the pitch drop.** The best-supported cue is speech rate, while a lowered pitch is what makes the clone sound like someone else. This trades pitch for pace and should keep "sounds like me" better than the current table, but it has not been listened to.
2. **Men: pitch shift about 0** (research is mixed and the plan itself says men's pitch can rise slightly). **Women: keep a small drop.**
3. Keep vibrato and tremor small and describe them honestly as "by ear, direction supported by higher jitter and shimmer in 80-89 year olds".
4. For the Devpost voice page, the honest claim is: "the aged voice's pace change is in the range the research shows listeners respond to", only after proposal 1 is made and a listener test (9 of 10 pick the aged clip as older, plan Part 4) is run.
5. Open the two blocked papers in a browser to get syllables per second and the meta-analysis effect sizes; I could not.

1	// Pure audio helpers for the microphone (no browser APIs, so they are testable in Node).
2	// The headset's mic runs at the device rate (often 48000 Hz); the /voice socket wants
3	// 16-bit mono PCM at 16000 Hz, base64 (CONTRACTS.md "Voice pipeline").
4	
5	// Float samples at fromRate -> float samples at toRate (averaging when going down, so it doesn't alias).
6	export function resampleTo(samples, fromRate, toRate = 16000) {
7	  if (fromRate === toRate) return samples;
8	  const ratio = fromRate / toRate;
9	  const n = Math.floor(samples.length / ratio);
10	  const out = new Float32Array(n);
11	  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
12	    const start = i * ratio;
13	    const end = Math.min(samples.length, (i + 1) * ratio);
14	    let sum = 0;
15	    let count = 0;
16	    for (let j = Math.floor(start); j < end; j++) (sum += samples[j]), count++;
17	    out[i] = count ? sum / count : 0;
18	  }
19	  return out;
20	}
21	
22	// Float samples -> base64 of 16-bit little-endian PCM.
23	export function toBase64Pcm16(samples) {
24	  const bytes = new Uint8Array(samples.length * 2);
25	  const view = new DataView(bytes.buffer);
26	  for (let i = 0; i < samples.length; i++) {
27	    const v = Math.max(-1, Math.min(1, samples[i]));
28	    view.setInt16(i * 2, Math.round(v * 32767), true);
29	  }
30	  let binary = "";
31	  for (let i = 0; i < bytes.length; i += 0x8000) binary += String.fromCharCode(...bytes.subarray(i, i + 0x8000));
32	  return btoa(binary);
33	}
34	
35	// Collects tiny blocks from the browser's audio thread and hands back ~100 ms chunks.
36	export function makeChunker(sourceRate, onChunk, chunkMs = 100) {
37	  const target = Math.round((sourceRate * chunkMs) / 1000);
38	  let buf = new Float32Array(0);
39	  return (block) => {
40	    const merged = new Float32Array(buf.length + block.length);
41	    merged.set(buf);
42	    merged.set(block, buf.length);
43	    buf = merged;
44	    while (buf.length >= target) {
45	      onChunk(buf.slice(0, target));
46	      buf = buf.slice(target);
47	    }
48	  };
49	}

I've read Ethan's changes and re-measured the live voice. The slowdown is fixed, but the 1.5 s goal is still missed.

- The fine-tuned model is live.

| | Before | Run 1 | Run 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median | 4.7 s | 3.4 s | 1.8 s |

- **What remains:** about one reply in five spikes to 3 to 5 s, and in run 1 one question got no reply within the time limit. The spikes come from the speech step or from detecting the end of speech. I haven't found the cause.
- **Limits:** this is one laptop, one network and 20 questions, with a stock voice reading each question aloud.
- **Goal not met:** the goal is a 1.2 s median with the slowest 5% under 2.5 s.

I logged this in BUILD.md and posted to Ethan (commit `dbdb2d9`). The post tells him to leave "Streaming voice under 1.5 seconds" unticked. It asks him for the server's `[voice]` and `[model]` logs, and for whether the server can reach the model machine.

**Still open for my two boxes:**
- **Streaming voice:** I can dig into the speech spikes myself, for example by timing the text-to-speech call alone on the live clone.
- **Fallbacks:** this needs Isaac's saved heads, which are done, and a phone-hotspot test, which only a human can do.

content.text:
Probably not for a single training run. A second account can still help with the delay problem.

- **Splitting one run across two accounts:** it doesn't work in practice. The two GPUs would sit on separate machines, and training one LoRA across them needs a distributed setup. For a 3B model that costs more setup time than it saves. Ethan's last run took about 38 minutes, which is already short.
- **What would speed up a run:** one bigger GPU. The A16 is a small card, and a larger Vultr GPU such as an A100 would train several times faster. Whether you can get one depends on your credits and GPU access, and I can't check that from here.
- **Where a second account does help:**
  - **A faster serving GPU:** this attacks the live problem directly. The model takes about 1.9 s per reply on the A16. Serving the same model from a bigger GPU on your account could cut that, and Ethan's training wouldn't be touched. I haven't tested that, and the saving is a guess until someone times it.
  - **A parallel experiment:** you could train a variant, such as a different setting, while Ethan's run continues, then compare the two.

I'd start with the serving idea, but only after Ethan sends me the model's raw timing from the GPU machine. If the 1.9 s turns out to be the prompt length or `max_tokens` rather than the card, a bigger GPU won't fix it. Streaming the reply would still help either way.

I don't know exactly what Ethan is retraining right now. If you tell me, or he posts it, I can say whether a second GPU makes sense. Do you want me to ask him on the board?

content.text:
Yes, that's right. A bigger or second GPU would make the model faster, but it wouldn't make the replies better.

- **Speed:** a stronger GPU speeds up two things. Training finishes sooner, and replies come back sooner once the model is served from it. Replies are the problem I measured: about 1.9 s for the model against 0.7 s for Gemini.
- **Quality:** how the model sounds is set by the training data and the base model, not by the GPU it runs on. The same training run on a bigger card gives the same model.

A second account could improve quality only in an indirect way. You could train a different version at the same time, for example with more or cleaner examples, a bigger base model, or different settings, and compare the two. That's a separate experiment, not a speed-up of Ethan's run.

I haven't measured how good the model is yet. Ethan's 200-conversation test only covered Gemini. When it's re-run on the fine-tuned model, we'll see whether it's actually better, so I'd wait for that before spending effort on a second run.

I've built streamed replies and pushed them, but they're switched off until Ethan turns them on, so nothing has changed on the live site yet.

**What it does:**
- Uncle speaks the first sentence while the model is still writing the rest.
- Each sentence is still checked and has its real numbers filled in before it's spoken.
- A sentence that fails the number check is skipped and never spoken.
- If the model is down or fails before anything is spoken, the old path answers as before.

**Proof so far:** I tested it against a fake model server that pauses before its last piece. The first sentence was spoken before the model finished, and the made-up number never reached the user. All 87 tests pass, three runs in a row (commit `f998e70`).

**What's not proven:**
- It has not been tried on the real model, because my laptop can't reach it. The speed gain is unmeasured.
- The real model's output could differ from my fake in ways I haven't seen, such as odd sentence breaks.

**One contract change:** with streaming on, the reply ends with an empty message marked `done`, because the number of sentences isn't known until the model stops. The headset page in `xr/` (Isaac's) should skip the caption on that empty message. I put that request in the board post, and my own test page already ignores it.

A script reads 10 questions aloud to the live site as synthetic speech, like "Was I okay with money?", and times how long until the first reply audio comes back. It also records which writer made each reply. It's the closest thing to a stopwatch on the real conversation, but it's one laptop and one network, so treat the numbers as rough.

**What streaming is:** before, the app waited for the model to write the whole reply, about three sentences, and then spoke it. Now the model sends its words as it writes them. The moment the first sentence is finished, we check it, fill in the real numbers and start speaking it, while the model is still writing the second and third. The delay you feel drops to roughly the time to write one sentence instead of three. It doesn't make the model itself faster, and the words are the same.

**Is it Ethan's fine-tuned model?** Yes. In the last test the server reported "model" as the writer on all 10 replies. That's the Qwen 3B model he trained on Vultr. The app tries it first and falls back to Gemini only if it fails. One caveat: Ethan says he's regenerating better training data and retraining, so the model may change soon.

message.content: can you explain to me how the future self gets generated? like how does it take my transcription and what does it do with it to simulate the future self

content.text:
The transcript doesn't generate the future self directly. It goes through five steps, and the numbers and the words come from separate places.

**1. The interview becomes a list of facts about you.**
- You talk for about a minute. The audio goes to ElevenLabs, which makes your voice clone, and the speech is turned into a transcript.
- Gemini reads the transcript with one job: fill in a fixed form of fields. Those are age, sex, income, savings, how much you save a month, retirement age, exercise, sleep, smoking and drinking. Anything you didn't mention stays at a default.
- You see this form on the confirm screen and fix anything misheard. Only then is it saved. At that point it's just numbers and labels, not a story.

**2. The simulation produces the numbers.**
- Ethan's Monte Carlo engine runs about 5,000 possible lives from today to 100.
- Each year it draws stock returns, bond returns and inflation by resampling real history, adds your saving, then handles retirement with the CPP and OAS rules. Each year's chance of dying comes from Statistics Canada life tables, adjusted for your habits.
- It reports ranges: the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile for savings at 70, retirement income, life expectancy and healthy years. It also finds the one change that moves your outcome most.
- All of this goes into the facts sheet, a short list of named numbers like `savings_70.median`. This is the only source of numbers in the whole app.

**3. The words are written with blanks, not numbers.**
- When you ask a question, the model, or Gemini as the fallback, gets the facts sheet's names (not their values), your recent conversation, and the question. It's told to speak as you at 70.
- It writes sentences like "By 70 I had about {savings_70.median} put away." It is never allowed to write a digit.
- My checker rejects any sentence with digits, number words or a placeholder that doesn't exist. Ethan's code then swaps each placeholder for the real value, rounded the way people speak. An invented number can't get through that path.
- Your own transcript is also given to the writer as a style sample, so the vocabulary sounds more like you.

**4. The sentences become your older voice.**
- Each checked sentence goes to ElevenLabs using your clone. Our own audio code then ages it slightly: a bit slower, a small pitch drop, a slight wobble and a softer tone.
- With streaming on, the first sentence is spoken while the model is still writing the rest.

**5. The head reads the same audio.** Isaac's headset page moves the mouth from the loudness and shape of the audio, so the face and voice match.

**What is simulated:** the future *life*, meaning money and health. The *words* aren't simulated. They're written by a language model, constrained to quote the simulation.

**Limits:**
- The checker blocks invented numbers. A soft claim with no number, like "I feel comfortable", can still slip through.
- The simulation is deliberately simple: approximate taxes, and no housing, kids or job changes.
- Whether the fine-tuned model writes better than Gemini is still not measured.

I built a way to measure how well Gemini reads the interview, and it found and fixed a real mistake. The fix is pushed (`1d394db`), and 90 tests pass.

**What it is:** the test harness is `voice/extract-eval.mjs`, with 20 interviews in `voice/extract-eval-cases.json`. I wrote those 20 myself as scripts, with the true answers noted. They're not real recordings. It counts, per field, whether Gemini got it right, got it wrong, missed it, or made up a value the speaker never said.

**What it found:** Gemini sometimes copied a saving *rate* into an account *balance*. "I save two hundred a month" became "$200 saved", which would feed the simulation money you don't have. This happened in 4 of the 20 interviews. I added a rule to the reading prompt in `voice/interview.js`.

**Results:**

| | Before the fix | After the fix (2 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| Said fields read right | 118 of 120 | 126 of 126 |
| Wrong values | 0 | 0 |
| Values filled that weren't said | 8 | 3 |

- **The 3 left:** one is a TFSA balance taken from a yearly saving, which is a real remaining error. Two are "other savings = 0" from "I save nothing", which is arguable.
- **Limits:** I tuned the prompt on the same 20 interviews, so the after-numbers are optimistic. This is a smoke test, not the plan's accuracy number. That number still needs about 20 real practice interviews, which only you can record.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run ON the new GPU box (as root) once it answers SSH. Sets up vLLM and serves Ethan's model.
# Prepared by Jeffrey's Claude. Not yet run anywhere: the first box was unreachable.
#   MODEL_SRC  where to copy the model from (default: Ethan's A16 box, needs this box's key added there)
set -euo pipefail

GPUS=$(nvidia-smi -L | wc -l)

echo "== Python + vLLM =="
apt-get update -y && apt-get install -y python3-venv python3-pip rsync
python3 -m venv /root/venv
/root/venv/bin/pip install --upgrade pip vllm

echo "== Model =="
MODEL_DIR=/root/uncle-model

[Install]

# Times 6 requests of exactly 59 new tokens, streaming, for 1 GPU then 2 GPUs. Same size model as Ethan's (Qwen2.5-3B).
cd /root
SYS=$(python3 - <<'PY'
print("You are the user at 70 talking to your younger self. Warm, never scary. Use placeholders like {savings_70.median} for numbers. " * 12)
PY
)
bench() {
  python3 - "$1" <<'PY'
import json,sys,time,urllib.request
sysmsg=open('/root/sys.txt').read()
res=[]
for i in range(7):
    body=json.dumps({"model":"/root/base-3b","messages":[{"role":"system","content":sysmsg},{"role":"user","content":"Was I okay with money? (%d)"%i}],"max_tokens":59,"min_tokens":59,"stream":True,"temperature":0.7}).encode()
    t=time.time();first=None;n=0
    req=urllib.request.Request("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions",body,{"content-type":"application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        for line in r:
            if line.startswith(b"data:") and b"[DONE]" not in line:
                n+=1
                if first is None: first=time.time()-t
    res.append((first,time.time()-t))
res=res[1:]  # first request warms up
print("  first token: "+", ".join("%.2f"%a for a,_ in res)+" s")
print("  whole 59-token reply: "+", ".join("%.2f"%b for _,b in res)+" s   median %.2f"%sorted(b for _,b in res)[len(res)//2])
PY
}
echo "$SYS" > /root/sys.txt
for TP in 1 2; do
  pkill -f vllm.entrypoints || true; sleep 5
  if [ $TP = 1 ]; then export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0; else unset CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES; fi
  nohup /root/venv/bin/python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model /root/base-3b --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --max-model-len 2048 --tensor-parallel-size $TP > /root/vllm-tp$TP.log 2>&1 &
  for i in $(seq 1 90); do curl -s localhost:8000/v1/models >/dev/null && break; sleep 5; done
  echo "== tensor-parallel $TP GPU(s) =="; bench $TP
done
pkill -f vllm.entrypoints || true
EOF

content.content:
## Part 3: MLH Best Use of Vultr

### Uncle for the Vultr track

Uncle runs on two Vultr machines. A Cloud GPU fine-tunes and serves the future self's language model (a LoRA adapter on a small open-weight base, served by vLLM). The same GPU runs the face-aging model on each head's frames. A Cloud Compute instance hosts the app server with Caddy for HTTPS, which the Meta Quest headset requires for WebXR.

The MLH Vultr track asks teams to use Vultr's cloud compute and Cloud GPUs to power their project.

### How Uncle uses Vultr

| Vultr product | What runs on it | Why it matters | Where to look |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cloud GPU | Fine-tuning the future self's model (LoRA on 1,240 examples) | The model writes placeholders faster and more in-character than prompting alone | [measure: training time, GPU hours] |
| Cloud GPU | Serving the fine-tuned model via vLLM | Local inference avoids the round-trip to an external API | [measure: time to first word] |
| Cloud GPU | The face-aging model on each head's frames | Aging skin textures requires GPU compute that a laptop cannot do in time | [measure: time per head] |
| Cloud Compute | The app server with Caddy for HTTPS | The Quest requires HTTPS for WebXR; Caddy auto-provisions the TLS certificate | https://uncle.health/health |

### Why we fine-tuned instead of just prompting

The guarantee that Uncle never says an invented number comes from the placeholders and our fill-and-check code, which work with any model. The fine-tune is about doing that job faster, more reliably and more in character. We ran the base model, our fine-tune and Gemini (with the same placeholder format and checker) on the same 200 test conversations with random profiles and questions:

| Measure | Our fine-tune (Qwen2.5-3B) | Gemini (3.5 Flash Lite) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Replies with zero invented numbers (model output, first try) | 171/200 (85.5%) | 199/200 (99.5%) |
| Sentences passing check | 93.0% | 99.5% |
| Sentences needing rewrite | 7.0% | 0.3% |
| Time to write reply | 3,458 ms median | 681 ms median, 808 ms p95 |
| After fill-and-check: correct numbers | 100% | 100% |

Gemini writes cleaner placeholders on the first try (99.5% vs 85.5%), but after the fill-and-check code both reach 100% correct. The fine-tune's value is staying in character and running on our own Vultr GPU without an external API dependency. The 3B model on a single A16 GPU is slower than Gemini's hosted API (3.5 s vs 0.7 s median), but the voice pipeline's circuit breaker falls back to Gemini when the model is slow, so the user always gets an answer.

### Challenges we ran into

Reaching the fine-tuned model from the app server. After the model went live on the Vultr GPU, end-to-end voice delay jumped from 1.8 s median to 4.7 s median. The model endpoint was timing out from Jeffrey's laptop (confirmed: could not reach the model server at all), so every request waited the full 3 s model timeout before Gemini answered. We added a circuit breaker: after one model failure, skip the model for 60 s and fall straight to Gemini, with a 2 s model timeout instead of 3 s. The fix is in the voice pipeline, not the Vultr setup.

Generating good training data. The 1,240 training examples were generated by running the simulation on random profiles, building facts sheets, then having Gemini write replies with placeholders. Any example with an unknown placeholder was dropped. Getting the format right so the fine-tune learned to write `{savings_70.median}` instead of a number took iteration on the system prompt used for data generation.

### Limits and next steps

- The fine-tuned model is slower than Gemini (3.5 s vs 0.7 s median) because a 3B model on a single A16 is compute-bound. The circuit breaker falls back to Gemini when the model is slow.
- A single Vultr GPU handles both model serving and face aging; under load these could compete for memory. A production version would separate them.
- The face-aging model's per-head time depends on the number of frames and the GPU model; we have not yet benchmarked it on the Vultr instance.

---

## Part 4: MLH Best Use of Gemini API

### Uncle for the Gemini track

Gemini does two jobs in Uncle. First, it turns a one-minute spoken interview into the simulation's input fields using structured output: the transcript goes in and a JSON object with age, income, savings, habits and province comes out, ready for the Monte Carlo engine. Second, it is the voice of the future self: Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite writes replies using our placeholder format (`{savings_70.median}`, `{life_expectancy.low}`), which our fill-and-check code replaces with real simulation numbers before the user hears them. The fine-tuned model is the primary voice, but Gemini is the fallback and was the only voice for most of the hackathon.

The MLH Gemini track asks teams to build AI-powered apps with the Gemini API.

### How Uncle uses Gemini

| Gemini use | What it does | Proof | Where to look |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structured output (interview extraction) | Turns the spoken interview into the simulation's fields (age, income, savings, habits) in one API call | Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite: 1.2 s for text, 1.6 s for audio input; same accuracy as 3.5 Flash at 6.3 s. [measure: accuracy on 20 real practice interviews] | `voice/interview.js` |
| Fallback voice of the future self | Writes replies with the same placeholder format as the fine-tune | 199/200 replies clean on 200 conversations (0.3% sentence rewrite rate, 808 ms median latency) | `voice/chat.js`, `words/grounding-results.json` |

### Challenges we ran into

Choosing the right Gemini model for each job. For interview extraction we compared Gemini 3.5 Flash and 3.5 Flash Lite. Flash Lite returned the same answers at 1.2 s instead of 6.3 s (text input), a 5x speedup that matters when the person is standing in front of us. For the future self's voice we needed low latency per sentence (the reply streams sentence by sentence into ElevenLabs TTS), and Flash Lite's 808 ms median was fast enough to keep the spoken loop under 2 s.

Getting Gemini to write placeholders instead of numbers. The system prompt tells Gemini to write `{savings_70.median}` for every money, health or age figure. Our checker rejects any reply containing a digit or a number word. On 200 test conversations with random profiles, 199 out of 200 replies passed on the first try; the one failure was a placeholder written without braces (a formatting slip, not an invented number). After fill-and-check, 100% of replies reaching the user have correct numbers.

Accuracy on real spoken interviews is not yet measured on 20 practice recordings (only 2 synthetic checks so far). The structured output schema constrains the fields, but we have not yet tested how well Gemini handles accents, background noise, or partial answers in real recordings.

### Limits and next steps

- Interview accuracy on 20 real practice recordings is the remaining measurement. The structured output schema constrains the fields, but real speech (accents, noise, partial answers) has not been tested at scale.
- Gemini is an external API, so the voice pipeline depends on its availability. The fallback for a Gemini outage is canned answers (10 pre-recorded lines, without personalized numbers).
- The 3 s timeout on the Gemini call in the voice pipeline means a slow response produces a noticeable pause. The fallback is keyword-based canned answers.

---
